blocks.heading: FROM GAME JAM TO VERTICAL SLICE
blocks.body:
Lightkeeper did not begin as Lightkeeper. It started as Fell Out, a small game-jam project built around a strange archipelago, its inhabitants, and a world hidden behind fog. We liked the setting enough to keep returning to it.

In 2024, Fell Out received concept funding from FFF Bayern. The job changed from “we made a fun little game” to “can this become an actual product?” We built a high-concept pitch, expanded the world, and tested exploration, gathering, traversal, progression and character interaction at a much larger scale.

Later that year the project, now Lightkeeper, received prototype funding. The prototype phase expanded the game again, but it also forced us to cut. The final vertical slice is the result of that path. This archive keeps the polished work next to discarded directions and technical tests because the interesting part is how the project changed every time we learned something new.

blocks.heading: EXPLORATION
blocks.body: The current slice combines traversal, environmental discovery, character interaction and progression across a strange archipelago.

blocks.heading: WORLD BUILDING WAS ALSO TOOL BUILDING
blocks.body: Building the world meant building terrain, progression and layout tools that let a small team iterate on scale, pacing and content.

blocks.heading: BEFORE THE VERTICAL SLICE
blocks.body: The technical test was where we searched for visual direction, world scale and traversal before committing to the current slice.

blocks.heading: FELL OUT
blocks.body: The game-jam idea became a formal high-concept pitch and received EUR 20,000 in concept funding from FFF Bayern in 2024.

blocks.heading: WHAT CHANGED
blocks.body: The project repeatedly exposed the difference between a promising prototype and a sustainable game. Systems expanded before the core loop was proven; later direction required cutting completed survival, farming, building and content work. The archive leaves those decisions visible.

blocks.heading: IN DEVELOPMENT
blocks.body:
KERN is the project I am currently trying to solve, which means most of this folder is design work in motion.

The central question is simple to state and difficult to make into a game: if the player encounters an anomaly they do not understand, how do they investigate it, infer what it does, and act on that knowledge without the interaction collapsing into a checklist?

The prototype footage, pitch material and institutional graphics are shown together because KERN’s fiction and mechanics are being designed at the same time.

blocks.heading: HOW DO YOU INVESTIGATE SOMETHING YOU DO NOT UNDERSTAND?
blocks.body: Tools should produce evidence rather than tick checklist boxes. Encounters need uncertainty, investigation needs risk, and solving an anomaly must lead to an action rather than only a label.

blocks.heading: WORLD IDENTITY
blocks.body: The identity work is institutional design for an organization that exists inside the Zone, not a detached logo exercise.

blocks.heading: CURRENT QUESTIONS
blocks.body: How much uncertainty can an investigation support? How should tools overlap? What persists after an encounter? This section remains intentionally open while the design changes.

title: KERN.GAME
heading: KERN
description: An investigative science-fiction game about entering an anomalous exclusion zone, observing things you do not understand, and learning their rules.

blocks.heading: A LOT OF MOVING PARTS
blocks.body:
Dronies was the project that moved me from product design into creative direction and project leadership. Over the course of the production I worked across the brand, story, comic issues, web and product design, merchandise, launch creative and the larger visual direction while coordinating a team of roughly 30 contributors.

My role changed with the needs of the project. At different points I was creative director, art director, producer and the communication layer between artists, designers, developers, marketing, community, operations and external partners. That included working with the Solana Labs team around the partnership and keeping the launch moving smoothly.

This was deeply collaborative work. I did not create every artifact shown here; individual creative credits are attached wherever the archive has them. My contribution was setting direction, producing key work myself and keeping many disciplines moving as one project.

blocks.heading: SCOPE / OUTCOME
blocks.body: Around 30 contributors worked across collection art, product, web, motion, brand, comics, merchandise, community, operations and the Bunker experience. The official collection contained 10,000 pieces and sold out in five minutes.

blocks.heading: CREDITS
blocks.body: Dronies was made by a large team. The creatives directory names contributors on individual artifacts where those records are available; the project breakdown focuses on my direction, production and hands-on design work without collapsing the team’s output into sole authorship.

blocks.heading: LESS FRICTION, MORE GAME
blocks.body:
We are using Flax for KERN and modifying the engine as the project exposes what we need from it. I care a perhaps unreasonable amount about how tools look and feel, but that attention has a practical purpose: every confusing interaction, awkward panel and lost selection breaks momentum for me and my co-founder. The less the editor gets in our way, the more time we have for the actual game.

This work is part design exercise, part production infrastructure. We are rebuilding our stack with the knowledge earned on earlier projects, focusing first on the interactions we repeat all day: transforms, hierarchy behavior, properties, docking, navigation and content browsing.

blocks.heading: TRANSFORM PRINCIPLES
blocks.body: Predictable handles, maintained mode and focus, correct axis visibility, precise feedback and less interaction-state loss.

blocks.heading: UPSTREAM / IMPLEMENTATION
blocks.body: The archive includes fork experiments, design proposals and contributions at different stages. Exact merged PR and commit links still need to be recovered; no fork-only change should be read as an official Flax feature.

blocks.heading: I DIRECTED A FILM
blocks.body: Daedalus Alpha is a seven-minute live-action short about a scientist confronting an apparent superintelligence - and the possibility that the intelligence speaking back may not be humanity's creation at all. I developed the concept over several months, then produced, directed and edited the film. The call sheet lists a 12-person production: nine unique crew members, including me, and three cast. We shot overnight from roughly 8 PM to 8 AM. It was one of the best creative experiences of my life, and a crash course in how much coordination, trust and stamina it takes to turn a written idea into a finished film.

blocks.heading: FROM IMAGE EXPERIMENT TO WORLD
blocks.body:
Daedalus began as Estafos & Suraya, a practical question about early generative-image tools: could a very small team turn unstable source images into a coherent narrative work instead of a folder of disconnected experiments?

The answer became a science-fiction story about two people who meet by accident on a planet that has trapped them, then discover that the mystery—and their own histories—are connected. I wrote and designed the 12-page comic, assembled and standardized the generated source material, built the pages in Figma, animated panels in Rive and helped turn the work into an interactive reader. The world later expanded into its own website, identity, merchandise and live-action film work.

blocks.heading: PROCESS
blocks.body: Story and script → generated source images → selection and cleanup → page design in Figma → panel animation in Rive → reader state machine and JavaScript progression. The difficult part was not producing images; it was forcing many imperfect inputs to behave like one authored world.

blocks.heading: SAME PROJECT, RADICALLY DIFFERENT ENTRY POINTS
blocks.body: A process-led post about creating the world, story, comic and animation in two months reached 9K views. A later post led with the personal reason for making the comic and reached 2.0M views, 3,417 upvotes and 236 comments. The work did not suddenly become two hundred times better; the framing gave people a human reason to enter it. That lesson now sits beside the production process because presenting a project is part of designing how it is understood.

blocks.heading: 12 PEOPLE / 12 HOURS / ONE NIGHT
blocks.body: The call sheet lists nine unique crew members, including me, and three cast. We worked through the night, from roughly 8 PM to 8 AM. I loved the intensity of it: directing performances, keeping departments aligned, protecting the idea while responding to what was actually happening on set, and then finding the final film again in the edit. It taught me more about production than any amount of planning could have.

blocks.body: The film was made for White Mirror, an anthology initiative produced by CHAPTR and The Culture DAO around human-machine collaboration. The wider project was presented in an official Venice Production Bridge session at the 80th Venice International Film Festival in 2023, moderated by Edward Saatchi of Fable Simulation and Philipp Nastaly of CHAPTR. That public record confirms the White Mirror presentation; it does not establish that Daedalus Alpha itself screened as part of the festival.

blocks.heading: THE FANTASY WORKED. THE LOOP DID NOT.
blocks.body:
Void Overdrive began as a single-player hoverbike prototype and quickly became a multiplayer test bed for an open world. We rebuilt the hoverbike and networking stack in Unreal as well as Unity to understand the tradeoffs between engines; Unity ultimately gave us a stronger path for moment-to-moment gameplay.

The unresolved problem was the game itself. Fast traversal and the pleasure of exploring a huge landscape pulled toward immediate action, while the experience we wanted—maintenance, costly pursuit and slow, methodical survival—pulled the other way. The visuals attracted a surprising amount of attention, but we never found a loop that reconciled those two fantasies. That tension is the most useful part of the project now.

blocks.heading: ATMOSPHERE AS THE PRIMARY MECHANIC
blocks.body:
Project Hypno was our first attempt at a horror game. I wrote the script in a week and we developed the prototype around the kind of deep, tactile simulation we loved in Voices of the Void, searching for a player fantasy that could support those mechanics rather than simply copying their surface.

The two-week project pushed me into unfamiliar territory: modeling, PBR materials, spatial sound design and the pacing of a horror atmosphere. It proved that we could create the mood, but not yet the larger gameplay framework that would sustain it.

blocks.heading: ONE WEEK, ONE SONG, ONE WORLD
blocks.body: I had been carrying this world around in my head for months, then gave myself one week to make it visible. I used a single song as the spine and pushed my Blender skills through every scene I could finish in that window. The mannequins are there because character design and animation were outside both my skill set and the scope; they look a little funny, and I’m fine with that. The project is rough, specific and still one of the concept pieces I’m happiest with.

blocks.heading: THE WRONG DIMENSION WAS THE LESSON
blocks.body:
Mighty Pebble came out of a list of deliberately small prototype ideas. The premise was a clicker game in which you play a god, gather resources directly from the world and buy upgrades that change what the world can produce.

The central mistake was prototyping it in 3D. Similar ideas such as Clicky Islands and Clickyland are clearer and more immediate because they embrace a 2D presentation. Realizing that was useful: 2D stopped feeling like a compromise and became an important part of how we think about future projects.

description: A 3D clicker-game prototype about a small god gathering resources, upgrading a world and learning why the same idea wanted to be 2D.

blocks.heading: FROM MUD TO AN EMPIRE
blocks.body:
Mattercraft asks what happens when a card game and clicker economy are combined with Little Alchemy. You begin with soil and mud, combine tools and materials, and gradually build a production system. The prototype made the crafting readable, but its only pressure came from managing an increasingly crowded field of cards.

In hindsight, it needed pushback: rats entering the system, furnaces consuming wood, cutters feeding tree production and relationships that gradually become a Factorio-like visual program. That missing pressure is the part I would explore if I return to it.

description: A 2026 card-based crafting prototype that mixes a clicker economy with Little Alchemy-style combinations and the beginnings of an automation game.

blocks.heading: ONE WEEK, A LOT OF FEEDBACK
blocks.body:
Spacekeeper was built in a week using Bezi AI to test how quickly AI-assisted development could turn an idea into something playable. The concept mixed space management with gathering and survival, wrapped in the readable daily rhythm of Stardew Valley.

The most valuable work was the feedback layer: UI response, in-world response, sound and the small pieces of juice that make an unfinished system feel legible. The core loop was still too weak for the scope the idea demanded, so we stopped at the prototype.

blocks.heading: A CONVINCING TRAILER IS NOT A GAME
blocks.body:
Fox Stories looked like a complete cozy adventure before that kind of errand-driven game had a familiar genre label. The prototype could be explored and items could be picked up, but the NPC interactions in the trailer were scripted and there was no real stealing, progression or sustaining gameplay loop.

The response was far larger than the prototype deserved. That attention pushed us to ask a harder question on every project afterward: what does the player actually do, and what role or profession lets them belong in the world?

blocks.heading: THE FANTASY TRAVELED FURTHER THAN THE PROTOTYPE
blocks.body: The response was exciting, but it exposed the gap between a world people wanted and a game we knew how to make. I keep the number here as evidence of resonance, not as proof that the design was solved.

blocks.heading: MY FIRST GAME, MADE IN ONE WEEK
LEARNING BY SHIPPING
blocks.body:
Moving On Express was my first game and my first time using Unity, Bolt and MagicaVoxel. I built almost everything—from the game design and voxel assets to the mechanical and technical implementation—in one week. The soundtrack was created by CillianCreates.

You play a mover loading a family’s belongings into a truck under a time limit. Speed matters, but damaged property comes out of your paycheck. It is a small idea, but shipping it taught me more than another month of abstract preparation would have.

blocks.heading: PLAN THE DAY, NOT THE ENTIRE UNIVERSE
blocks.body:
Yesterday starts with a drawer containing everything you could do, then asks you to choose what actually belongs today. Tasks can be organized into Must Do, Communications and general lists, placed into scheduled work blocks, and rolled forward when unfinished. Reflection, due dates, theme controls and dense keyboard navigation are part of the same idea: make daily planning more honest without turning it into another management job.

The desktop app is built with Electron, React and TypeScript and runs on Windows and macOS.

description: An opinionated offline daily planner that turns a backlog into a realistic day through focus lists, scheduled work blocks, rollover and keyboard-first control.

blocks.heading: CHORDS WITHOUT BREAKING FLOW
blocks.body: MIDI Clip Builder is designed for learning and composing with chords quickly from the keyboard. A single note can become a chord, and the tool adjusts the result as you move between keys, chord systems and progressions. The goal is not to hide music theory; it is to make the rules immediate enough that they can be learned through use.

blocks.heading: A SOUND LIBRARY THAT UNDERSTANDS ITS FOLDERS
blocks.body:
Sonilabs indexes large local sound libraries and makes them searchable by filename, metadata, folder, format, tags and source. Sounds can be previewed against a waveform, adjusted for gain, trimmed to a selected region and queued for export without leaving the library. Manual tags and notes sit beside the structure already present in filenames and folders.

The app is local-first and built with Tauri, React, TypeScript, Rust and SQLite. Audio, cache data, analysis and export jobs stay on the machine.

description: A local-first desktop sound-library browser, previewer, processor and exporter for large audio collections.

blocks.heading: THE PART BETWEEN A SCREEN RECORDING AND A SHAREABLE CLIP
blocks.body:
QuickClipper is a focused desktop clip editor for the repetitive work that happens after capturing a screen recording: choose the useful region, set in and out points, crop or resize the frame, keep the export under a file-size target, and get the result out quickly. The interface keeps the source pool, viewer, inspector and timeline visible at once so a small edit does not grow into a full editing session.

The current app is built with Tauri and React. It produces Windows installers, supports signed GitHub releases and updates, and includes video, audio and audio-only export paths.

title: CLIPPER.APP

description: A focused Tauri + React desktop clip editor for trimming, crop/resize, file-size targets and fast export.
